title: Split names with Flash Fill
how: Type the first name for the first row, move to the next cell and press ⌘E. Excel fills the rest of the column from your pattern, and the same trick works for joining names or pulling out employee IDs.

title: Fill blank cells with the value above
how: Select the column, go to Edit > Find > Go To (⌃G), click Special and choose Blanks. Type = and press the up arrow, then press ⌃Return to fill every blank at once.

title: Find hard-coded numbers in a model
how: Select the sheet, open Home > Find & Select > Go To Special and choose Constants with only Numbers ticked. Every typed-in number is selected, so you can give them a fill colour and check none should be a formula.

title: Copy only the visible filtered rows
how: After filtering, select the data and press ⌘⇧Z to select visible cells only, then copy and paste. Hidden rows are left behind instead of sneaking into your paste.

title: Select all formulas or errors to audit
how: Open Home > Find & Select > Go To Special, choose Formulas and tick only Errors. Excel selects every #N/A, #DIV/0! and #REF! cell so you can fix them one by one.

title: Spot mismatched numbers with row differences
how: Select two columns, such as the books figure and the bank figure, and press ⌃\. Excel selects every cell in the second column that differs from the first, so you can colour them.

title: Paste values only
how: Copy the cells, then press ⌘⇧V to paste just the values without formulas or formatting. On older builds use ⌃⌘V and choose Values.

title: Apply a % increase to many cells at once
how: Type 1.1 in a spare cell and copy it, select the prices, press ⌃⌘V and choose Multiply. Every price goes up by 10% in place; use Divide with 100000 to convert rupees into lakh.

title: Turn rows into columns with Transpose
how: Copy the range, click the destination, press ⌃⌘V and tick Transpose. Months that ran across the top now run down the side.

title: Paste formats, widths or skip blanks
how: Press ⌃⌘V after copying and choose Formats, Column widths or tick Skip blanks. Skip blanks stops empty cells in the copied range from wiping out data already in the destination.

title: Paste a live picture of a range
how: Copy a range, go to Edit > Paste Special and choose Linked Picture (or Home > Paste > Paste as Picture > Linked Picture). The picture updates when the source cells change, which is handy on dashboards.
availability: Mac: partial. The Camera tool is Windows only; use Paste Special > Linked Picture.

title: Build custom number formats
how: Press ⌘1, choose Custom and type a format such as ₹#,##0;[Red]-₹#,##0;"-" to show rupees, negatives in red and a dash for zero, or 0.0,"K" to show thousands as K. Formats can only scale by thousands, so for lakh or crore figures divide by 100000 or 10000000 in a helper column.

title: Hide cell contents with ;;;
how: Select the cells, press ⌘1, choose Custom and type ;;; as the format. The value is still there for formulas and shows in the formula bar, but nothing displays in the cell.

title: Use Indian comma grouping (12,34,567)
Jump around with names and the Name Box
how: Select a cell or range, type a name such as GST_Rate in the Name Box left of the formula bar and press Return. Later pick that name from the Name Box dropdown to jump straight there.

title: Create names from headings in one go
how: Select a table including its header row, then go to Formulas > Create from Selection and tick Top row. Each column gets a name matching its heading.

title: Build state-to-city dependent dropdowns
how: Name each city list after its state (for example Maharashtra), then set the city column's Data Validation list source to =INDIRECT(A2). Picking a state in A2 limits the city dropdown to that state's cities.

title: Make dropdowns that grow automatically
how: Point the Data Validation list source at a Table column, or at a spill range such as =$H$2# where H2 holds =SORT(UNIQUE(B2:B500)). New items appear in the dropdown without editing the rule.

title: Validate PAN length and block duplicates
how: Select the column, go to Data > Data Validation, choose Custom and enter a formula such as =AND(LEN(A2)=10,COUNTIF($A$2:$A$500,A2)=1). Excel rejects any PAN that is not 10 characters or is already listed; use LEN(A2)=15 for GSTIN.

title: Add input messages and error alerts
how: In Data > Data Validation, use the Input Message tab to show a hint like "Enter date as DD-MM-YYYY" and the Error Alert tab to set Stop, Warning or Information. Users see the hint as soon as they click the cell.

title: Show trends inside cells with sparklines
how: Select the monthly numbers, go to Insert > Sparklines and choose Line, Column or Win/Loss, then pick the cell to hold it. Each row gets a tiny chart that fits next to the figures.

title: Highlight the whole row with a formula
how: Select the data from row 2, choose Home > Conditional Formatting > New Rule, use a formula such as =$E2="Pending" and pick a fill. The $ before the column letter makes the entire row light up, not just one cell.

title: Highlight duplicate or unique values
how: Select the column and choose Home > Conditional Formatting > Highlight Cells Rules > Duplicate Values. Switch the dropdown to Unique to mark the one-off entries instead.

title: Add data bars and icon sets
how: Select the numbers and choose Home > Conditional Formatting > Data Bars or Icon Sets. You get an instant visual of which branch or salesperson is ahead without building a chart.

title: Flag due and overdue dates
how: Select the rows and add a formula rule such as =$D2<TODAY() in red and =$D2-TODAY()<=7 in amber. Payment due dates change colour on their own each day.

title: Insert checkboxes in cells
how: Select the cells and choose Insert > Checkbox. Each cell holds TRUE or FALSE, so you can count ticks with =COUNTIF(B2:B50,TRUE) for a to-do or attendance list.

title: Convert a range into an Excel Table
how: Click inside the data and press ⌘T (⌃T also works), then confirm the header row. Formulas, formatting and charts now expand automatically as you add rows, and you can switch on a Total Row from the Table tab.

title: Add slicers to a Table
how: Click inside a Table and choose Table > Insert Slicer, then tick the fields you want. Clicking a slicer button filters the Table, which is easier for colleagues than filter arrows.

title: Freeze the header row
how: Go to View > Freeze Top Row, or click the cell below and right of what should stay put and choose View > Freeze Panes. Headings stay visible while you scroll through thousands of rows.

title: View two sheets side by side
how: Use Window > New Window to open a second view of the same workbook, then Window > Arrange to place them side by side. You can also drag the split bar or use View > Split to see two parts of one sheet.

title: AutoFit column width with a double-click
how: Point at the border to the right of a column letter until the cursor changes, then double-click. The column resizes to fit its longest entry; select several columns first to fit them all.

title: Move rows without overwriting
how: Select the rows, hold ⇧ and drag the selection border to the new spot. A green line shows where they will be inserted, and nothing gets overwritten.

title: Copy a sheet by dragging its tab
how: Hold ⌥ and drag the sheet tab sideways, then let go. Excel creates a copy such as "Apr (2)", ready to rename for the next month.

title: Build a contents sheet with hyperlinks
how: Add a Contents sheet, select a cell, press ⌘K, choose This Document (Place in This Document) and pick the target sheet. Add a "Back to contents" link on each sheet so nobody gets lost in a 30-tab workbook.
availability: The Navigation pane is Windows only. On a Mac use a hyperlinked contents sheet.

title: Jump to the edge of your data
how: Press ⌘ with an arrow key to jump to the last filled cell in that direction, and add ⇧ to select everything on the way. On a 50,000-row export this beats scrolling.

title: Fill one entry into many cells
how: Select all the cells, type the value once and press ⌃Return. The same entry, such as "Pune" or a formula, goes into every selected cell.

title: Start a new line inside a cell
how: While typing in a cell, press ⌥⌘Return (or ⌃⌥Return) to break the line. Useful for addresses with a flat number on one line and the locality on the next.

title: Insert today's date or current time
how: Press ⌃; to type today's date and ⌘; for the current time. Unlike =TODAY(), these are fixed values that will not change tomorrow.

title: Add totals with AutoSum
how: Select the cell below a column of numbers and press ⌘⇧T, then Return. Select a block plus an empty row and column first to total both directions at once.

title: Repeat actions and lock references
how: Press ⌘Y to repeat your last action, such as inserting a row or applying a fill. While editing a formula, click a reference and press ⌘T to cycle through $A$1, A$1, $A1 and A1.

title: Open Format Cells quickly
how: Select the cells and press ⌘1. The Format Cells dialog opens with number formats, alignment, borders, fill and protection in one place.

title: Toggle filters on and off
how: Click inside the data and press ⌘⇧F to add filter arrows to the header row. Press it again to remove them and clear all filters.

title: Select, insert and delete rows and columns
how: Press ⌃Space to select a column or ⇧Space to select a row. Then press ⌃I to insert or ⌘- to delete.

title: Show all formulas at once
how: Press ⌃` (the key left of 1) to show formulas instead of results across the sheet. Press it again to switch back.

title: Check part of a formula with F9
how: While editing a formula, select one part of it, such as a VLOOKUP inside an IF, and press F9 (fn+F9 on a laptop) to see its result. Press Esc afterwards so the formula is not overwritten with the value.

title: Trace and watch formulas
how: Use Formulas > Trace Precedents and Trace Dependents to draw arrows to related cells, and Formulas > Evaluate Formula to step through a calculation. Add key cells to Formulas > Watch Window to keep an eye on them from any sheet.

title: Use the ribbon from the keyboard
how: Recent Mac builds show KeyTips, letters over each ribbon command, so you can reach commands without the mouse. Check Excel's Help or the Mac keyboard shortcut list for how to turn them on in your build.
availability: New on Mac; check your build

title: Customise the Quick Access Toolbar
how: Click the ... at the right end of the Quick Access Toolbar and choose More Commands, or go to Excel > Preferences > Ribbon & Toolbar. Add the commands you use daily, such as Paste Values or Freeze Panes.

title: Type long text with AutoCorrect shortcuts
how: Go to Excel > Preferences > AutoCorrect and add an entry, for example replace "abcpl" with "ABC Private Limited, Mumbai". Typing the short code then expands to the full name.

title: Create an April-to-March custom list
how: Go to Excel > Preferences > Custom Lists and add Apr, May, Jun through Mar. Type Apr in a cell and drag the fill handle to get months in financial-year order.

title: Fill weekdays, months or growth series
how: Type a start date, select the range and choose Home > Fill > Series, then pick Weekday or Month, or Linear or Growth with a step value. You get working days only or month-end dates without typing them.

title: Rejoin or split text with Fill Justify
how: Select a single column of short text lines, widen the column and choose Home > Fill > Justify. Excel joins the lines into fewer cells, or splits long text into lines when the column is narrow.

title: Split data with Text to Columns
how: Select the column and choose Data > Text to Columns, then split by a delimiter such as a comma. Running it with no changes also converts numbers stored as text into real numbers.

title: Fix numbers stored as text
how: Select the cells with the green triangle, click the warning icon and choose Convert to Number. For a whole column, Paste Special > Multiply by 1 or =VALUE(A2) does the same.

title: Remove duplicate rows
how: Click inside the data and choose Data > Remove Duplicates, then tick the columns that define a duplicate. To keep the original untouched, use =UNIQUE(A2:C500) in a new spot instead.

title: Clean extra and non-breaking spaces
how: Use =TRIM(CLEAN(A2)) to remove extra spaces and hidden characters from imported data. If spaces remain, they are usually non-breaking spaces from web or ERP exports: use =TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A2,CHAR(160)," ")).

title: Find with wildcards and Find All
how: Press ⌘F, open the advanced Find options and use * for any text and ? for one character, for example *Pvt* to catch every private limited company. Click Find All, then ⌘A in the results list to select all matching cells.

title: Find and replace formatting
how: Press ⌃H, expand the options and use the Format buttons to search for a fill colour or font and replace it with another. Handy when someone has marked rows yellow and you want them green.

title: Remove blank rows safely
how: Filter a key column for (Blanks), select the visible rows and delete them, then clear the filter. Avoid Go To Special > Blanks on the whole range, which can delete rows that are only partly empty.

title: Fix DD/MM and MM/DD date mix-ups
how: Select the imported date column, choose Data > Text to Columns, click Next twice, choose Date with DMY and Finish. Dates like 05/04/2026 become 5 April 2026 instead of 4 May.

title: Show % of total or month-on-month change
how: In a PivotTable, right-click a value and choose Show Values As > % of Grand Total, or Difference From with the previous month as the base item. Add the same field twice to show the amount and the % side by side.

title: Group pivot dates by month, quarter or FY
how: Right-click a date in the PivotTable and choose Group, then select Months and Quarters. For an April-March year, add a helper column =YEAR(A2)+(MONTH(A2)>=4) to the source and use it as the FY field.

title: Let Excel suggest PivotTables and charts
how: Click inside your data and choose Insert > Recommended PivotTables or Insert > Recommended Charts. Pick one of the suggestions as a starting point and adjust from there.

title: Split a pivot into one sheet per item
how: Put a field such as Branch in the Filters area, then choose PivotTable Analyze > Options > Show Report Filter Pages. Excel creates a separate sheet for each branch in seconds.

title: Control GETPIVOTDATA and drill-down
how: To get normal cell references when you click a pivot cell, turn off Generate GetPivotData (on a Mac look under Excel > Preferences > Calculation, or the PivotTable Analyze > Options dropdown). To stop people double-clicking into the raw data, untick Enable show details in PivotTable Options.

title: Filter pivot dates with a Timeline
how: Click the PivotTable and choose PivotTable Analyze > Insert Timeline, then pick the date field. Drag across months or quarters to filter the report.

title: Control several pivots with one slicer
how: Insert a slicer on one PivotTable, then right-click the slicer and choose Report Connections. Tick the other PivotTables built from the same data, and one click filters them all.

title: Get quick charts without Quick Analysis
how: Quick Analysis does not exist on a Mac. Select the data and use Insert > Recommended Charts, or Home > Conditional Formatting for quick visuals.
availability: Windows only. On a Mac use Insert > Recommended Charts.

title: Ask questions with Analyze Data
how: Click inside a Table and choose Home > Analyze Data, then type a question like "total sales by region". Excel suggests charts and PivotTables you can insert with one click.

title: Forecast with one click
how: Select a date column and a values column, then choose Data > Forecast Sheet and set the end date. Excel builds a forecast table and chart with upper and lower bounds.

title: Find the target with Goal Seek
how: Go to Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek, set the profit cell to your target, such as ₹10 lakh, by changing the sales cell. Excel works backwards to the sales figure you need.

title: Build an EMI sensitivity table
how: Write =PMT(rate/12,months,-loan) once, lay out interest rates down a column and tenures across a row, then use Data > What-If Analysis > Data Table. You get every EMI combination for a home or car loan in one grid.

title: Compare cases with Scenario Manager
how: Go to Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager and add Best, Expected and Worst scenarios with different input values. Click Summary to get a side-by-side report on a new sheet.

title: Plot two scales with a combo chart
how: Select the data, choose Insert > Chart > Combo, and set the smaller series (such as margin %) as a line on the secondary axis. Revenue in crore and margin % then sit clearly on one chart.

title: Link a chart title to a cell
how: Click the chart title, type = in the formula bar, click a cell holding text such as ="Sales for "&B1 and press Return. The title updates whenever the cell changes.

title: Control charts with hidden rows
how: By default charts skip hidden rows, so filtering a Table changes the chart. To keep hidden data in the chart, open Chart Design > Select Data > Hidden and Empty Cells and tick Show data in hidden rows and columns.

title: Build a waterfall for a profit bridge
how: Select the items from revenue down to net profit and choose Insert > Chart > Waterfall. Click the total bars and choose Set as Total so they start from zero.

title: Make a simple Gantt chart
how: Build a stacked bar chart from start dates and durations, then set the start-date series to No Fill. Alternatively, use conditional formatting with =AND(E$1>=$B2,E$1<=$C2) on a date grid.

title: Polish a dashboard
how: Untick Gridlines and Headings on the View tab, then select shapes and use Shape Format > Align to line them up. Use linked pictures (Paste Special > Linked Picture) to place live snapshots of ranges.
availability: Mac: partial. The Camera tool is Windows only; use Paste Special > Linked Picture.

title: Protect a sheet but leave inputs open
how: Select the input cells, press ⌘1, go to Protection and untick Locked. Then choose Review > Protect Sheet so only those cells can be edited.

title: Hide formulas and set edit ranges
how: Press ⌘1, go to Protection and tick Hidden before protecting the sheet, so formulas do not show in the formula bar. Allow Edit Ranges lets specific people edit specific areas.
availability: Mac: partial. Hiding formulas works; Allow Edit Ranges may not be available, check your build.

title: Use comments, notes and @mentions
how: Use Review > New Comment for a threaded discussion and type @ plus a colleague's name to notify them by email. Use Notes (Review > Notes) for a plain sticky note that needs no reply.

title: Filter without disturbing co-authors
how: In a shared workbook on OneDrive or SharePoint, choose View > New Sheet View, then sort and filter freely. Your view does not change what colleagues see.
availability: Microsoft 365, OneDrive or SharePoint files; check your Mac build

title: Restore an earlier version
how: Save the file to OneDrive so AutoSave is on, then go to File > Browse Version History. Open an older version and restore it if someone has overwritten your work.

title: Read cells aloud to proofread
how: Speak Cells reads numbers aloud as you move down a column, which helps when checking figures against a printout. If your Mac build does not have it, select the cells and use macOS Spoken Content (System Settings > Accessibility > Spoken Content).
availability: Check availability on your Mac build

title: Enter records with a Data Form
how: Add Form to the Quick Access Toolbar or ribbon, click inside the list and open it to enter one record at a time in a dialog. If your build does not offer it, type straight into the blank row below a Table.
availability: Check availability on your Mac build

title: Link to sheets and cells
how: Select a cell, press ⌘K, choose This Document and pick a sheet and cell reference. Or use =HYPERLINK("#'Mar'!A1","Go to March") to build links with a formula.

title: Print neatly on one page wide
how: Use Page Layout > Print Titles to repeat the header row on every page, and Page Layout > Scale to Fit with Width set to 1 page. Check the breaks in View > Page Break Preview and set a Print Area for just the part you need.

title: Write readable formulas with LET and LAMBDA
how: Use LET to name parts of a formula, for example =LET(gst,B2*18%,B2+gst). Save a LAMBDA in Formulas > Define Name to create your own function such as =GSTAMT(B2).

title: Use whole columns without the zeros
how: Wrap a range in TRIMRANGE or use a dot reference like A:.A so the formula stops at the last filled cell. =UNIQUE(A:.A) then gives a clean list without a trailing 0.

title: Look up with two or more criteria
how: Join the criteria with &, for example =XLOOKUP(G2&H2,A2:A500&B2:B500,C2:E500), to match on both region and product. Returning C2:E500 brings back three columns at once.

title: Filter with AND and OR conditions
how: Multiply conditions for AND and add them for OR, for example =FILTER(A2:D500,(B2:B500="North")*(D2:D500>100000)). Use + instead of * to return rows that meet either condition.

title: Split text with TEXTSPLIT and TEXTBEFORE
how: Use =TEXTSPLIT(A2,",") to split a comma list across cells, and =TEXTBEFORE(A2,"@") or =TEXTAFTER(A2,"@") to pull out the parts of an email address.

title: Unpivot and combine files in Power Query
how: Choose Data > Get Data > From Folder to combine every monthly CSV in a folder, or select month columns in the editor and choose Unpivot Columns. Next month, drop the new file in the folder and click Data > Refresh All.

title: Collect several copies with a clipboard
how: The Office Clipboard pane that holds many copied items is not in Excel for Mac. Use a clipboard manager app on your Mac to keep a history of copied items and paste them one by one.
availability: Windows only. On a Mac use a clipboard manager app.

title: Pin files and open read-only copies
how: Pin workbooks you use daily from File > Open Recent so they stay at the top. To avoid accidental changes, save with Read-only recommended in the save options, or open a copy instead of the original.

title: Change Excel settings worth changing
how: Go to Excel > Preferences to set the default font, turn off gridlines for new sheets, and shorten the AutoRecover interval under Save. Dark mode follows your Mac's appearance, and Excel > Preferences > General lets you turn it off for Excel.

title: Place a picture inside a cell
how: Choose Insert > Pictures > Place in Cell, or use =IMAGE("https://...") with a web address. The picture moves and sorts with its row, which suits product lists and staff photos.

title: Turn PDF tables into Excel
how: Data > From PDF is not on a Mac. Open the PDF in Claude in Excel or Copilot and ask it to extract the table into a sheet, then check the totals against the PDF.
availability: Windows only. On a Mac use Claude in Excel or Copilot to extract the table.

title: Try new list functions
how: Newer functions such as lists in cells, HAS, HASANY, HASALL and FLATTEN are in preview. Join the Microsoft 365 Insider programme if you want to try them, and avoid them in files shared with colleagues until they are generally available.
